prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling frequency standards with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18
for the conception and leadership of the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos

statement.case_for: I still rank gamma-ray burst afterglows (B033) and IceCube (B010) highest on discovery-centred grounds, but the discussion has made me weigh what can actually be defended in a single prize. Optical lattice clocks (B043) have the broadest and most stable support in the room (two first places, six rankings), a clean two-person attribution (Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and first strontium clock, Ye for the record accuracy), independent confirmation in several laboratories and species, and a measurable consequence: 1e-18 uncertainty, tests of constants and relativity, and the pending redefinition of the second. IceCube (B010) is the other half because it opened a genuinely new window on the universe: a diffuse TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrino flux, then the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 associations and the Galactic plane. That is a discovery in the sense I use the word, and it is more fundamental to our understanding of the cosmos than an instrument advance alone. Pairing a precision-measurement achievement with an astrophysical discovery gives two distinct achievements and keeps the union at three people.
statement.case_against: Naming only Halzen for IceCube is the weakest point. The result belongs to a collaboration of hundreds, AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES laid groundwork, and Karle and Yoshida have real claims; any single name will look arbitrary to part of the community. B043 is also more an advance in measurement than a conceptual breakthrough, and it sits close to the earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes. And a two-part prize with a lone laureate on one half is unusual. If the committee decides IceCube cannot be credited cleanly, I would rather drop that half than invent an artificial trio.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as the opening of a new observational window, with Halzen as the conceiver and leader, while admitting the decisive work is collective and several leaders are not captured by a trio.
responses.response: I agree on the science and share the attribution worry, but I would turn it into a decision about how many names IceCube can carry. You and Olsson both identify Halzen as the evident intellectual leader, whereas Karle's and Yoshida's roles are described more vaguely in the supplied material, including in my own opening. Crediting Halzen alone is cleaner than a trio that I admitted is hard to defend. I disagree only if you can show that Karle's detector and analysis leadership is decisive in a way that cannot be separated from Halzen's.

responses.point: Olsson places magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a sharp prediction followed by experiment, a clear before and after that opened a new platform of correlated and topological phases.
responses.response: The theory-plus-experiment structure is attractive and I ranked B029 fourth myself, and the attribution to Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero is natural. My reservation is maturity. The experiments date from 2018, the origin of the superconductivity is unresolved, and Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, Cao and Dean make the credit less tidy than the opening suggests. I would keep B029 as a leading alternative and revisit it in a few years, rather than prefer it to two achievements with decades of confirmation.

responses.point: Kroll and Lindroth put optical lattice clocks first, stressing that fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 and many-atom interrogation is the kind of advance in what we can measure that deserves recognition.
responses.response: I largely agree and now treat B043 as the anchor of my configuration. My earlier ranking of it fifth reflected the view that it is a technical advance and that Hall and Hansch were already honoured in 2005. But the lattice-clock idea, removing Doppler and recoil shifts while using many atoms, is distinct from the comb, and the independent confirmation in Sr, Yb and Hg is unusually strong. My remaining qualification is that measurement-science prizes should be tied to demonstrated fundamental results, so the citation should stress accuracy and its consequences, not only the technique.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks circuit QED fourth but flags that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits makes another circuit award premature.
responses.response: I agree with the timing argument and it is one reason I do not put B023 in my configuration, even though Johansson ranks it first and Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff all have claims. A second superconducting-circuit prize right after 2025 would look redundant, and the four-name credit problem makes it harder still.

uncertainties: Whether Halzen alone can be defended for IceCube, or whether Karle and Yoshida must be added and another part dropped to stay within three people.
How much weight the committee gives to GRB afterglows (B033), which only Pearce and I ranked and whose credit (Costa, Frontera, Kulkarni; van Paradijs deceased) is historically delicate.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene is mature enough given the unresolved origin of its superconductivity.
My recollection of the IceCube and BeppoSAX credit history comes from memory rather than verification against the supplied nomination text.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not involve any shortlisted candidate.
